1:
An oracle against Moab delivered to Judah raises the question who it was for, and two voices answer alike. Henry supposes the prophet never went among the Moabites but delivered it to his own people, for three reasons: to show that judgment beginning at the house of God does not end there, and that worshippers of false gods are accountable to the God of Israel; to prove his care of his own and his enmity to their enemies; and because a prophecy fulfilled within three years would confirm his mission and encourage the faithful to rely on the rest. Calvin reaches the same conclusion by exclusion, since the prophet neither addressed the Moabites nor sent them a written communication, and gives as his first reason that men seeing cities overturned and kingdoms succeed one another should not think the world governed by the blind violence of fortune.

Calvin adds what makes the oracle bitter, that Moab descended from Abraham's nephew, so kinship demanded some friendly intercourse, and that no relationship restrained them from harassing the Jews whenever they could, which he takes for a savage disposition. On the date they largely agree. Henry expects fulfilment within three years, by Shalmaneser about the taking of Samaria in Hezekiah's fourth year, or else by Sennacherib ten years later. Clarke prefers the first and puts the delivery in Hezekiah's first year, noting that the English margin dates it fourteen years earlier than the two chapters before it. Wesley divides the fulfilment between the Assyrian and the Babylonian empires.

Clarke makes two further observations. This chapter and the next form one entire prophecy, in his judgment very improperly divided; and Jeremiah has happily taken much of it into his own longer oracle against the same people, so that comparing the two rectifies several transcribers' mistakes in both. Ellicott remarks instead on the obscurity of Moabite history and the difficulty of identifying these towns, in striking contrast to the world-drama of the burden of Babylon; what light there is must come from elsewhere, and he draws on the inscribed Moabite stone found at Dibon, which records a tribute of sheep reckoned by hundreds of thousands, the revolt, and the king's boast of taking Nebo and slaying seven thousand.

That the cities fell at night is pressed by one and dismissed by another. Henry finds a reason in it, that the inhabitants were probably given to ease and dwelt securely as the men of Laish did, and draws the lesson that we should lie down as those who do not know what a night may bring forth; he adds that as the country feeds the cities so the cities protect the country, and neither may say it has no need of the other. Clarke grants the circumstance is somewhat unusual but judges it not material enough to be so strongly insisted on. Wesley says only that it means suddenly and unexpectedly. Keil and Delitzsch supply the quarrel's background, the tribute paid from Moabite flocks to Samaria and its refusal when Ahab died.

Where Moab goes in its distress is a matter of translation. Gill, Clarke and Ellicott all deny that the first word is a place name, taking it for the house or temple, very likely that of Chemosh; Clarke reports a proposal to join it with the next word as one name, supported by two versions but no manuscript, and observes that the place evidently puzzled scribes and editors alike. Ellicott identifies the high places from the same inscription, and takes Nebo for a city named after the deity, not the mountain. On the shaved heads Clarke cites an ancient historian for whom cutting the hair in mourning was universal except among the Egyptians, while Ellicott thinks the practice perhaps sacrificial in origin and notes it was forbidden to Israel as belonging to the worship of other gods.
5:
Whose heart cries out for Moab is disputed. Gill takes it for the prophet's, pitying them as fellow creatures though they were enemies, and notes that others, with the Targum, refer it to the Moabites lamenting their own country. Clarke settles it against the prophet on textual grounds, since the Greek and the Chaldee read his heart rather than mine, and renders it the heart of Moab crying within her. Ellicott keeps the prophet, touched with pity though a stranger to Moab and belonging to a hostile people. Henry keeps him too, adding that we do not know how soon it may be our own turn to drink the same cup. Wesley grants the pity grudgingly, allowing that Moab is a most vile nation.

Calvin answers a third way, by making it a matter of method rather than of feeling. He raises the objection himself: it seems strange that the prophet should bewail the Moabites when he ought rather to have lamented the ruin of the Church and rejoiced at the fall of her enemies. His reply is that the prophets customarily assume the character of those whose calamities they foretell, exhibiting their condition as if upon a stage, which strikes harder than instruction delivered directly. He allows they may also have shuddered at God's judgments on the wicked, but thinks the simpler explanation better. Henry draws the pastoral conclusion, that God's ministers should be of a tender spirit and not desire the woeful day.

The heifer of three years old is read four ways. Clarke reports from an ancient naturalist that in cattle alone the female's voice is deeper than the male's, so a heifer's lowing is the apter image for mourning; he then admits the expression is very short and obscure and interpreters differ widely. Ellicott hears a wild scare, the animal as yet untamed by the yoke. Calvin applies the figure not to the flight but to its destination, a town in full vigour that had never felt the yoke and never been attacked, to which men run as the place furthest from danger. Henry hears simply a heifer lowing for her calf.

The clause about the fugitives rests on a marginal reading. Ellicott notes that the received text gives instead that his bars reach to Zoar, and grants this is not easy to connect with the context; Keil and Delitzsch adopt that harder reading, rendering it bolts. On the two places named Ellicott admits ignorance twice. No city bearing the first name has been identified, and he supposes the ascent so called was the approach to a Moabite sanctuary, the name perhaps indicating a staircase of boards; the second is as little known, its name meaning two caverns. His point is that the fugitives reaching it are met by the cry of destruction, all is over. Wesley glosses that cry as the sound men make when they are just falling into the pit.

The desolation is then counted in water, goods and blood. Gill offers alternatives for the dried waters, a drought or a defiling with blood, and preserves a report of hot springs in that region running some bitter and some sweet. Henry observes that famine is the usual effect of war, and that if an army encamps on green fields their greenness is soon gone; on the wealth carried to the brook of willows he cannot decide whether the owners take it there to hide it or the enemy to pack it home, and draws the lesson that those eager to lay up this world's goods little consider how soon they may be taken. Ellicott finds a grim pun in the last place named, its form altered towards the word for blood, and takes the lions either literally or as figures for the invader.
